1. The animation shows how inflation wears down what an income check can buy. Each bar is a different starting month, from 1947 to Aug 2006, and shows how far a first check's buying power has fallen 20 years later. The label says US consumer prices (CPI-U) typically rose 3.1% a year over those stretches.

2. In frames 1 to 3, a highlighted band of starting months in the 1980s shifts and a reference line appears. By frame 4 the bars are all filled in and a line is drawn at 80.7%. In frames 5 and 6 a row of ten small crates appears and about eight of them light up.

3. The image says a "typical rising check after 20 years" is worth 80.7% of the first check. That is about 8 of 10 crates. In other words, even a check that rises over time typically buys only about four-fifths of what the first check did after 20 years. I can't tell exactly how the "rising check" is built, because the frames don't say. The bars also vary a lot by starting period, and the figure is US history, "not a forecast."

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer could take away that inflation matters over a long retirement and that the two payout options should be compared with it in mind. The frames never say which option to choose.

5. That takeaway is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the historical pattern and the 80.7% figure. It doesn't recommend any action.
